title: Class 6 Maths Surface Area and Volume Explained (with Case Studies + Quiz)
meta_title: Class 6 Maths Surface Area and Volume + Quiz
meta_desc: Learn class 6 maths surface area and volume: find volume of cubes and cuboids and surface area from nets, with solved case studies and a free online quiz.
excerpt: Volume tells you what fits inside a box; surface area tells you what covers the outside. Here is the Class 6 chapter made simple, with two solved real-life case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
My nephew in Jaipur once spent twenty minutes trying to wrap a cricket bat in gift paper and gave up because the paper kept falling short. That kitchen-table disaster is exactly what class 6 maths surface area and volume is about: how much space a box holds versus how much paper you need to cover it. Get those two ideas separated in a child’s head early, and the whole chapter stops feeling confusing.

The NCERT chapter sticks to shapes children can actually hold — cubes and cuboids — so every idea here can be shown with a matchbox, a Rubik’s cube, or a rooftop water tank. Let me walk through what the chapter really asks, and then solve two real case studies the way the practice book does.

Volume and surface area are not the same question

This is the single mix-up I see most. Volume answers ‘how much fits inside?’ — the rice in a container, the water in a tank. Surface area answers ‘how much covers the outside?’ — the paper on a gift, the tiles on a wall. One is about the inside, the other about the skin. They even use different units, which is the clue that gives them away.

The unit is the giveaway

Volume is measured in cubic units (cm³, m³) because you are filling space in three directions. Surface area is measured in square units (cm², m²) because a surface is flat — two directions only. If a child writes cm² for a volume, the maths is already off, no matter how neat the number looks.

Volume of a cuboid and a cube

A cuboid’s volume is simply length × breadth × height, and the answer is always in cubic units. For a box 8 cm long, 5 cm wide and 3 cm tall, the volume is 8 × 5 × 3 = 120 cubic centimetres. The order of the three numbers does not matter — multiply them and label the answer in cubic units.

A cube is the easy cousin: all three edges are equal, so its volume is side × side × side. A Rubik’s cube of edge 6 cm holds 6 × 6 × 6 = 216 cm³. No new rule — just equal edges.

Surface area from the six faces (and nets)

Here is where a net earns its keep. Unfold a cuboid box flat and you get six rectangles: two matching ones for top and bottom, two for front and back, two for the sides. Add the areas of all six and you have the surface area. Doing it face by face — rather than memorising a formula — is exactly how the class 6 maths surface area and volume chapter builds the idea.

For a cube it is even neater. All six faces are identical squares, so the surface area is 6 × (side × side). A cube of edge 4 cm has surface area 6 × 16 = 96 cm².

Case study 1: wrapping a gift box

Read this the way the case-study book sets it up. Meera buys a rectangular jewellery box that is 20 cm long, 12 cm wide and 5 cm high. She wants to gift-wrap it and also know how much cotton will fit inside.

  • How much cotton fits inside? (volume) 20 × 12 × 5 = 1200 cm³. The box holds 1200 cubic centimetres.
  • How much paper covers it? (surface area) Add the six faces — top and bottom 2 × (20 × 12) = 480; front and back 2 × (20 × 5) = 200; two sides 2 × (12 × 5) = 120. Total = 480 + 200 + 120 = 800 cm².

Same box, two different questions, two different units. Meera would buy paper by the 800 cm², never by the volume — a slip worth catching now.

Case study 2: filling a water tank

A cuboidal water tank on a Pune rooftop is 2 m long, 1 m wide and 1 m deep. How much water does it hold? Volume = 2 × 1 × 1 = 2 cubic metres. Since 1 cubic metre is 1000 litres, the tank holds 2000 litres — roughly a family’s water for two days.

Now suppose the tank must be painted on its four side walls to seal it. That is a surface-area question, and it uses only the four vertical faces, not all six. This is the kind of twist the case studies drill: reading the passage carefully to decide which faces actually count.

A quick word on getting it right

The counter-intuitive bit for most eleven-year-olds is that a bigger surface area does not mean a bigger volume. A flat pizza-box shape can have a large surface area yet hold very little. In my experience the fastest cure for the volume-versus-surface-area muddle is to keep asking one question aloud: ‘inside or outside?’ Inside means cubic units; outside means square units.

Try the quiz, then the case studies

The eight-question quiz below covers volume of cubes and cuboids, surface area from faces, and telling the two apart — the exact skills in this chapter. Try it, read the explanations for anything your child misses, and when they are ready for full passage-style questions with worked answers, the case-study e-book at the end is the natural next step.

quiz.title: Class 6 Surface Area and Volume Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on volume of cubes and cuboids, surface area from faces, and telling the two apart. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 6 surface area and volume of cubes and cuboids

questions.q: What is the volume of a cuboid 5 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm?
questions.explanation: Volume of a cuboid is length × breadth × height: 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cubic cm.

questions.q: A cube has an edge of 4 cm. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: A cube’s volume is side × side × side: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cubic cm.

questions.q: How many faces does a cube have?
questions.explanation: A cube has 6 identical square faces — that is why its surface area is 6 × side × side.

questions.q: What is the surface area of a cube with edge 3 cm?
questions.explanation: Surface area of a cube is 6 × (side × side) = 6 × 9 = 54 square cm.

questions.q: Volume is always measured in which kind of units?
questions.explanation: Volume fills space in three directions, so it is measured in cubic units such as cubic cm.

questions.q: Surface area is measured in which kind of units?
questions.explanation: A surface is flat — two directions — so surface area is measured in square units such as square cm.

questions.q: A packing box is 10 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm. How much does it hold?
questions.explanation: Volume = 10 × 5 × 4 = 200 cubic cm, the space inside the box.

questions.q: You want to know how much paper covers the outside of a box. Which do you find?
questions.explanation: Covering the outside is a surface-area question. Volume would tell you what fits inside, not what wraps around it.

faq.q: What is the difference between volume and surface area in Class 6?
faq.a: Volume tells you how much fits inside a shape and is measured in cubic units (cm³). Surface area tells you how much covers the outside and is measured in square units (cm²). Inside versus outside is the quickest way to remember which is which.

faq.q: How do you find the volume of a cuboid?
faq.a: Multiply its three dimensions: volume = length × breadth × height. For a box 6 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm the volume is 6 × 4 × 2 = 48 cubic cm. For a cube, all edges are equal, so volume = side × side × side.

faq.q: How is a net used to find surface area?
faq.a: A net is the shape unfolded flat. A cuboid opens into six rectangles; add the areas of all six and you get the surface area. It helps children see why a cuboid has three pairs of matching faces instead of relying on a formula.

faq.q: Why do volume and surface area use different units?
faq.a: Volume fills space in three directions, so its units are cubic (cm³). A surface is flat and stretches in only two directions, so its units are square (cm²). If the units do not match the quantity, something has gone wrong in the working.
